content: In biological taxonomy, the term type refers to the specific reference point that permanently links a name to a taxon. Depending on the nomenclature code applied, a type can be a specimen, a culture, an illustration, a description, or even another taxon. The concept of a type is essential for ensuring consistency and clarity in the naming of organisms, but its application varies between botany and zoology. Botany In botanical nomenclature, a type (or nomenclatural type) is the element to which the name of a taxon is permanently attached. A botanical name, by itself, is merely a phrase, and its meaning depends on the type to which it is linked. In botany, a type is typically either a specimen or an illustration. A specimen is a physical plant (or part of a plant) that is preserved and curated in a herbarium or a similar facility for fungi. In some cases, an illustration may serve as the type, particularly in historical contexts where transporting or preserving plant specimens was challenging. For example: Detailed botanical drawings or paintings from the early days of plant taxonomy often served as types when physical specimens were unavailable or lost. Microscopic organisms, which are difficult to preserve as specimens, may have their types represented by detailed illustrations. It is important to note that a type only fixes a name to a single representative of the taxon. It does not define the boundaries or circumscription of the taxon. For instance, the name Taraxacum officinale (common dandelion) is linked to the same type regardless of whether the species is considered a single large species or divided into many smaller species. The taxonomist determines the circumscription of the taxon in their publications. Additional notes on botanical types: Only species or infraspecific taxa can have their own types. For taxa described after January 1, 1958, illustrations cannot serve as types. A genus typically shares its type with one of its species, often referred to informally as the type species, though this term has no formal standing under the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN). Similarly, a family shares its type with one of its genera, often called the type genus. The ICBN outlines various types in Article 9, with the holotype being the most significant. Other terms like clonotype appear in botanical literature but lack formal recognition under the ICBN. Zoology In zoological nomenclature, a type refers to a specimen or taxon that serves as the objective reference point for the application of a name. A name-bearing type provides the standard by which the name of a nominal taxon is determined. Definitions A type specimen is an informal term for an individual or fossil that serves as a name-bearing type for a species. For example, the type specimen for Homo neanderthalensis is Neanderthal-1, discovered in 1856, which includes a skullcap, thigh bones, part of a pelvis, ribs, and arm bones. A type species is the species that serves as the name-bearing type for a genus or subgenus. A type genus is the genus that serves as the name-bearing type for a family-group taxon. The type series includes all specimens cited in the original description of a taxon unless explicitly excluded. Use of Types When describing a new species, biologists may examine multiple specimens, but the formal rules of the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN) require the designation of a single type specimen, known as the holotype. The holotype is typically stored in a museum or collection for future reference. The type description should include comparisons with closely related species and details about the type's storage location. The geographical origin of the type specimen is referred to as its type locality. In addition to the holotype, other formally defined types include: Paratype: Additional specimens listed in the type series but not designated as the holotype. These are not name-bearing types. Neotype: A specimen designated as the type when the original holotype is lost, destroyed, or never existed. Syntype: Any of two or more specimens cited in a species description when no holotype was designated. Lectotype: A specimen later selected from a set of syntypes to serve as the single type specimen. Paralectotype: Any remaining syntypes after a lectotype has been designated. These are not name-bearing types. Hapantotype: A special case in protists where the type consists of multiple specimens representing different life stages, treated collectively as a single entity. The need for these various types arises because many species descriptions date back centuries, when holotypes were not always designated or preserved. The ICZN, established in 1961, now requires a type specimen for new species, but many older species lack types. For example, Homo sapiens does not have a designated type specimen, as its taxonomic status is not in question, and the ICZN prohibits the designation of a neotype unless there is an exceptional need. In some modern cases, type specimens have been released back into the wild after their description, such as the Bulo Burti Bush-shrike (Laniarius liberatus). In such cases, DNA samples may serve as a reference, but a neotype may need to be designated if questions about the species arise in the future. There are many other terms with the suffix -type (e.g., allotype, cotype, topotype), but these are not formally regulated by the ICZN and are often obsolete or idiosyncratic. Type Species Each genus must have a designated type species. The term genotype was historically used for this purpose but is now avoided due to its association with genetics. The type species permanently links the generic name to a name-bearing type. While the type species ideally exemplifies the genus's characteristics, this is not a requirement. If the type species is later found to belong to a pre-existing genus, the original genus name may become a synonym unless an exception is granted by the ICZN. Type Genus A type genus is the genus from which the name of a family or subfamily is derived. Like type species, the type genus is not necessarily the most representative but is often the earliest described or best-known genus. Family names based on type genera that later become synonyms do not need to be changed.
